group_info.article:
## Definition
A geospatial strategy is a plan that sets out what spatial data an organization needs, for what purpose, with what priority, and how it will build and use it. Geospatial data governance is the system of rules, roles, and responsibilities that governs how this data is produced, managed, and shared throughout its life cycle. The two concepts come together in what is known as a spatial data infrastructure (SDI): the framework that brings policies, standards, technologies, and people together so that spatial data is available, reliable, and shareable.

## Categories
Governance is usually organized around several areas: ownership and stewardship (who owns each dataset and who looks after it); standards (data formats, models, and coordinate reference systems); metadata, which documents the source, accuracy, and currency of the data; master and reference data, such as neighborhood boundaries, addresses, and the road network, on which all other data depends; and the policies that govern access, privacy, and sharing.

## Approaches
A strategy is usually built in successive steps: assessing current data maturity, identifying the gaps between the current state and the need, ranking initiatives by value and effort, and then setting a roadmap and performance indicators to measure progress. Governance draws on international standards, most notably the ISO 19100 series issued by technical committee ISO/TC 211 since its founding in 1994, and the open OGC standards for exchange and interoperability.

## A brief history
The concept emerged at the national level in 1994, when the United States established the National Spatial Data Infrastructure (NSDI) by executive order, after it became clear that multiple government agencies were producing the same data at duplicated cost and in conflicting formats. In 2007, the European Union issued the INSPIRE Directive to harmonize spatial data across its member states. In 2018, the United Nations Committee of Experts on Global Geospatial Information Management (UN-GGIM) adopted the Integrated Geospatial Information Framework (IGIF) as a guide for countries building their national systems.

## Why it matters
Without strategy and governance, spatial data turns into scattered effort: duplicated datasets, conflicts between departments, and investments not tied to clear goals. With them, data becomes a unified, reliable enterprise asset that serves many entities and uses and complies with national requirements.

group_info.article:
## Definition
Geospatial data design is the definition of how geographic phenomena are represented in a database: which entities there are, what their attributes are, and how they relate to one another spatially and descriptively. Enterprise architecture is the broader structure that defines where this data is stored, how it moves between systems, and how it reaches applications and users.

## Categories
Spatial data is represented by two main models: the vector model, which describes phenomena as points, lines, and polygons, such as buildings, roads, and boundaries; and the raster model, which divides space into regular cells, as with aerial imagery and elevation models. Data models range from two-dimensional to three-dimensional, such as CityGML, adopted by the OGC as a standard for representing cities in 2008. At the architecture level, a distinction is made between operational databases that serve daily work and data warehouses that bring different sources together for analysis.

## Approaches
Design usually passes through three stages: a conceptual model that defines entities and relationships in business language; a logical model that translates them into tables, layers, and topological rules; and a physical model that defines how data is stored and indexed in the database system. Spatial databases rely on special indexes such as the R-tree, introduced by Antonin Guttman in 1984, which allow fast location-based searches across millions of features.

## A brief history
In 1970, Edgar Codd introduced the relational model for databases, which became the basis for storing attribute data. For many years spatial data was kept in files separate from databases, until databases that support spatial types directly appeared. The OGC Simple Features standard then unified how geometries are represented and stored, making it possible to exchange data between different systems without rebuilding it.

## Why it matters
Good design determines the data's ability to serve the organization for years: the right model keeps data consistent, makes querying and analysis easier, and accommodates growth without rebuilding. The effects of poor design show up later in duplicated data, slow systems, difficult integration, and rising maintenance and development costs.

## Definition
Geospatial data migration is moving data from one system, format, or coordinate reference system to another while preserving its accuracy, attributes, and relationships. Integration is connecting systems so that they exchange data and update it regularly, rather than each dataset remaining isolated in its own system.

## Categories
Integration is usually classified into three levels: data-level integration, in which data is moved and transformed through extract, transform, and load (ETL/ELT) processes; service-level integration, in which data is made available through services and APIs without being copied; and application-level integration, in which systems share the same processes. In migration, a distinction is made between converting between formats, transforming between coordinate reference systems, and a full move from one platform to another.

## Approaches
Established approaches include mapping data models between source and target before the move, transforming coordinate reference systems with documented parameters, verifying after migration by comparing counts, lengths, areas, and topological relationships, and automating updates with scheduled processing pipelines. For data exchange, open OGC standards such as the Web Map Service (WMS) and Web Feature Service (WFS) are used, alongside open formats such as GeoJSON.

## A brief history
From the start, this field has been bound up with the problem of differing coordinate reference systems. Many countries and regions have historical local geodetic datums, and the position of the same point in two different datums can differ by tens or even hundreds of meters: enough to put a building in the wrong place or one land parcel on top of another. Accurate transformation between datums, and unifying them in modern datums compatible with global systems, has therefore become an essential step in any migration project. With the spread of web-based data exchange at the turn of the millennium, integration shifted from copying files by hand to services that serve data directly from its source.

## Why it matters
With multiple systems inside a single organization, integration becomes a condition for getting value from data. Without it, data stays isolated, outdated, and duplicated, and updating it depends on error-prone manual effort. Disciplined migration and good integration ensure that data moves without loss, stays current, and is securely available to everyone who needs it.

group_info.article:
## Definition
Geospatial data quality is the degree to which spatial data is fit for the purpose for which it is used. Data is not good or bad in absolute terms, but only to the extent that it meets the requirements of its use: a map suitable for city-level planning may not be suitable for defining property boundaries. Quality control covers measuring quality, improving it, and maintaining it with every update.

## Categories
The international standard ISO 19157 defines the elements of geographic data quality, most notably: completeness (whether all features are present, with nothing missing or extra); logical consistency (whether the data follows the rules of the model and its topological relationships); positional accuracy (how close the coordinates are to the true location); thematic accuracy (the correctness of classifications and attributes); and temporal quality (how current the data is and whether its dates are correct).

## Approaches
Quality is controlled through several approaches: automated topological checks to detect overlapping polygons, gaps, and disconnected lines; comparing a sample of the data with a more accurate source to measure positional error; validation rules for attribute values; documenting metadata that records the source, accuracy, and date of each dataset; and version management that keeps a record of every change and who made it.

## A brief history
One of the oldest quality standards in this field is the National Map Accuracy Standards adopted by the United States in 1947, which required at least 90% of tested points to fall within a specified error limit depending on the map scale. With the shift to digital data, positional accuracy alone was no longer enough, and the need arose to measure completeness, consistency, and currency as well, which ISO brought together in the ISO 19157 standard, published in 2013.

## Why it matters
Quality is a precondition for any use of spatial data, because analyses, applications, and decisions can be no more accurate than the data they rest on. Low-quality data leads to misleading results and extra rework costs, while reliable, current data builds confidence in the outputs and makes them auditable and reviewable.

group_info.article:
## Definition
Geospatial analytics is a branch of geographic information science concerned with studying phenomena through their locations and spatial relationships. It rests on a principle formulated by the geographer Waldo Tobler in 1970, known as the First Law of Geography: "Everything is related to everything else, but near things are more related than distant things." Spatial data is therefore not treated as independent numbers, but as values whose meaning is shaped by their location.

## Categories
Spatial analysis is usually classified into four levels: descriptive analysis, which shows the distribution and density of a phenomenon; exploratory analysis, which reveals clusters, hotspots, and unexpected patterns; inferential analysis, which tests statistically whether a pattern is real or random; and predictive and prescriptive analysis, which estimates what will happen and suggests the best location, route, or scenario.

## Approaches
Key approaches include overlay analysis, which combines multiple layers to identify suitable locations; proximity and buffer analysis; network analysis to calculate shortest routes and service areas; spatial interpolation such as kriging to estimate values at unmeasured locations; measures of spatial autocorrelation such as Moran's I, introduced by Patrick Moran in 1950; and multi-criteria analysis, which balances different factors with defined weights.

## A brief history
The work of the physician John Snow in 1854 is the best-known early example of the power of spatial analysis. He mapped cholera deaths in London's Soho district, noticed that they clustered around a water pump on Broad Street, and so provided early evidence that the disease spread through water, at a time when the prevailing view was that it spread through foul air. In the 1960s, Roger Tomlinson developed in Canada the first computerized geographic information system, for land inventory and classification. In 1969, the planner Ian McHarg published his book Design with Nature, which established the layer overlay method in land suitability analysis. Kriging originated in the 1950s with the mining engineer Danie Krige, who used it to estimate gold reserves in South Africa, and it went on to become a core tool in the earth and environmental sciences.

## Why it matters
Because most planning and operational decisions are tied to place, geospatial analysis provides them with an objective basis: it reveals what tables and raw numbers do not show, such as distribution, concentration, and proximity; it turns the comparison of alternatives from judgment into measurement; and it makes it possible to track the impact of decisions over time.
